source.title: On the Dynamics of Delayed Generalization in Linear Models
source.authors: Atreya Vedantam; Nataraj Das; Chandrashekar Lakshminarayanan

record.tranche_reason: The study reports delayed generalization in a linear model, but refines the scope of grokking-like claims: the delay depends strongly on the test distribution and support-vector imbalance, and the authors say it is not grokking in its usual form.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own test-accuracy results for synthetic separable data and MNIST. Its discussion of other explanations and cited studies is not recorded as results. It does not test small algorithmic datasets, training-set-size effects, circuit formation, initialization-scale or weight-norm switches, or optimizer/numerical ablations.
record.test_reason: The paper reports its own train and test accuracy curves for a linear model on synthetic separable data and for a small ReLU net on MNIST 4-vs-9. These bear on whether grokking-like delays arise on non-algorithmic data (V3). It also argues that the delay comes from support-vector imbalance plus a boundary-concentrated test set. The authors state they do not see grokking in its usual form, so this restates the scope of V3 rather than replicating it.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate. The authors show delayed generalization needs no depth or compositional structure: it arises in a linear model with learnable bias under full-batch GD. The late bias is set by support-vector imbalance, giving a generalization time at least exponential in |log δ| on boundary-concentrated test data. The delay is small on ordinary test data, and they 'do not observe grokking in its usual form'. On MNIST only the output-bias behaviour is verified, with no accuracy delay.
record.recipe_differences: The original studies concern small algorithmic tasks and grokking in neural networks. This paper analyzes and trains a linear classifier with bias using full-batch gradient descent and exponential loss on linearly separable synthetic data, then tracks output-bias behavior in a one-hidden-layer MNIST network.
record.method_sensitivity: Test distribution (ordinary versus concentrated near the boundary), support-vector class balance, and population class balance change the reported delay.

fits_no_version.finding: Plain GD with exponential loss on separable data passes through three phases: population-dominated, support-vector-dominated unlearning, then generalization. The learnable bias converges to −log δ, set by support-vector imbalance. Generalization time on near-boundary test points is at least exponential in |log δ|.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Delayed generalization can arise in linear models from a mismatch between the learnable bias and the max-margin separator, driven by support-vector class imbalance and visible only on test points near the decision boundary.

record.code_released: The checklist says code is provided in supplementary material; no URL is stated.
record.problems: The authors report no error bars or seed-based uncertainty statistics. The synthetic delay depends on a concentrated test distribution and support-vector imbalance; the paper says it does not observe grokking in its usual form. The MNIST experiment only tracks the output bias mechanism and uses standard test data, whose accuracy stays near 1.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported test-accuracy result was left out.

untested.parts: No algorithmic datasets and no training-set-size sweep (N=2000 in all synthetic runs).
No circuit or progress-measure analysis. Hidden features on MNIST are not described.
No initialization-scale or weight-norm manipulation and no lazy-to-rich transition. No text or molecule data. Init is fixed at zero (synthetic) or PyTorch default (MNIST).
No weight decay (explicitly left open), no critical dataset size, no ungrokking.
No comparison of algorithms across runs.
No optimizer or precision ablation. All runs use plain full-batch GD in float64.

record.verdict_notes: The delay appears under plain full-batch GD in float64 with no adaptive optimizer. This is incidentally consistent with delays not requiring the V7 artifacts, but the study runs no ablation, so V7 gets no verdict. The test distribution Pconc is deliberately constructed to sit near the boundary. The MNIST support vectors are computed in input space, while the bias dynamics act on hidden features. There are no error bars or multiple seeds; one data seed (42) is used. Neither original source is this study.

versions.untested_parts: No small algorithmic dataset, training-set-size sweep, or test of whether delay grows as the training set shrinks.
No analysis of Fourier circuits, gradual circuit formation, removal of memorizing components, or continuous mechanism-based progress measures.

Tests delayed accuracy on synthetic non-algorithmic data and reports MNIST results, but does not test text or molecule data, initialization-scale changes, weight-norm interventions, or a lazy-to-rich transition.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data.
No weight decay or other low-norm bias intervention, efficiency comparison, critical dataset size, or ungrokking test; the paper leaves weight decay open.
No comparison of identifiable algorithms learned across runs.
No controlled optimizer or numerical-precision comparison testing whether grokking delays disappear when those choices are controlled.

rows.subject: linear model with bias
rows.operation_detail: Measured training and test accuracy during training on synthetic separable data without planted support vectors.
rows.value: It rises in Phase 1, dips in Phase 2, and recovers only after about 10^5 epochs.
rows.note: The text describes this as the concentrated-test result; no exact accuracy values are given.
rows.check: The delay appears only on the constructed boundary-concentrated test set (Pconc). Test accuracy rises, dips, then recovers after about 10^5 epochs; it does not jump from chance after training saturates. Appendix C says this run has no planted support vectors and only illustrates test-distribution dependence. 'Observed' overstates it.

rows.note: The paper contrasts this rapid result with delayed recovery on the concentrated test distribution.

relationships.condition: Synthetic 2D separable data, linear model, evaluated on the boundary-concentrated test set Pconc
relationships.reason: A late recovery appears (R1; R3 recovers after 10^6 epochs) but needs a near-boundary test set. It is switched by support-vector imbalance in the data (R4 balanced: no delay), not by training regime. The authors say it is not grokking in its usual form.
relationships.display_finding: Late recovery occurred after 10^6 epochs on a boundary-concentrated test set, while balanced support vectors removed the delay; the authors distinguished this behavior from usual grokking.

relation.reason: Its own synthetic and MNIST accuracy trajectories directly measure the presence or absence of delayed generalization.

tranche.reason: The study supplies an alternative mechanism and results qualifying delayed generalization through support-vector composition and evaluation distribution, while explicitly distinguishing its behavior from usual grokking.

source_check.notes: R2's Pconc comparator is explicitly supported by the paired evaluation in Figure 1 and Section 5.2. MNIST training data were filtered for separability; the standard test split was unchanged. Several pack fields are abbreviated, but the relevant source passages are readable.

statements.correction: Tested synthetic setting: large delayed recovery on Pconc with imbalanced support vectors; balanced S(350,350): no delay; ordinary P: accuracy reaches 1 within about 10^2 epochs; standard binary-MNIST test accuracy: near 1. General necessity of boundary concentration and support-vector imbalance: not established.
statements.problem: The reported contrasts are accurate, but 'requires' overstates necessity: the paper establishes a large delay in its constructed setting and describes the delay as small otherwise.
